articles.title: Mick Gordon On How He Helped to Make Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2’s Climactic Boss Fight “Big and Bombastic”
articles.summary: Mick Gordon On How He Helped to Make Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2’s Climactic Boss Fight “Big and Bombastic”
articles.body:
If you were making a sequel to Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun and wanted to inject a bit of extra boom into the boomer shooter, then you probably wouldn’t look any further than Mick Gordon. The legendary Aussie composer has been soundtracking videogames for about two decades, but it was his face-melting work on 2016’s Doom and 2020’s Doom Eternal that really established his monster guitar riffs as the perfect way to fire up fans of first-person shooters. It seemed a no-brainer, then, that developer Auroch Digital would enlist Gordon to add his signature heavy touch to the climactic boss fight at the end of Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2. Ahead of the game’s release this week, IGN caught up with Gordon to get an insight into how his curtain-dropping contribution to the shooter sequel’s soundtrack came about.

IGN: How did you come to be involved with Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2? Were you familiar with the first game?

Mick Gordon: Yeah, definitely. So, I sent the team an email after the first Boltgun, and I said, “Hey, this game is really cool. There are a lot of boomer shooters out at the moment, but I think what you guys have done with it feels really good. It feels really fun to play. And you've obviously combined this pixelated, sprite-based, first-person shooter boomer shooter thing with the Warhammer 40K universe in what seems to be the most obvious idea that nobody else had ever thought of. Really, really great job.”

So, I had a bit of a relationship with them from that moment. And when they were doing the sequel, they shot me an email. They're like, "You know what? We've got this giant boss battle at the end, and it's on a scale that did not appear in the first game, and we want to have some music for it that kind of matches that scale, something that's really big and bombastic and silly. Would you like to do it?"

And of course, I was like, "Yeah, I'd absolutely love to." I've always wanted to, but I've never been involved in the Warhammer universe. I've always wanted to stray into that territory, but I've never [been] given an opportunity to until this one came along. So, there's the first-person shooter aspect, there's the Doom-inspired first-person shooter aspect, there's the pixelated aspect, there's this giant evil-looking demonic battle boss battle thing, and then there's the Warhammer thing. So, I mean, how would you not say yes to that? It's like a match made in heaven, really, isn't it?

IGN: When something like this kind of falls in your lap, do you start completely from scratch or do you have a folder on your MacBook that's labelled "Sick First-Person Shooter Riffs" and you just kind of scoop some of those out and start sculpting with them?

Gordon: No, definitely not. My job on every single project is to try to come up with a unique voice that suits that project and that project only. I like to think about these things as something that I come up with exists in a sphere in the universe, and that sphere belongs to that thing and that project, and that is unique in that space. When I'm coming up with something else, I can't push that sphere into the space that that other sphere exists in. Do you know what I mean? I have to come up with something that takes up its own space.

Now, of course, people will say, "Well, we've listened to your music. It sounds like you did this, sounds like you did this, you did this." I know you can never completely divorce yourself from your own tastes and input. So, I understand that. But my goal is to try and work with the team to come up with something unique that fits the music's purpose for that specific project alone. So, I don't just have like a bunch of [pre-existing] riffs or ideas that I would put into this game, and this game, and this game. That's not my job. My job is to sit with the team and try to find what makes their thing unique and really just explode that out [in an] extreme sort of way musically.

IGN: As part of your process for creating your track, ‘Ascent of the Arkifane’, did you actually play the boss battle itself?

Gordon: It can be difficult because often games aren't fun to play until they are finished and ready to release. You know what I mean? And often because of the rapid development on these games, there are builds being done several times a day. So, it can be very difficult for a team to send me a stable build to actually work with.

Instead, what they do is send me capture footage that the QA department puts together for me. And the QA people, it's their sole job to play the game all day. So, they are really good at it, and they're really good at making it look like it's how it's going to be. And that's perfect. That's all I need. They will send me that. They will send me screenshots. They will send me concept art. I will have conversations with the developers and things. But I love videos. Videos are the best.

Why I love the videos is I take the video when I get it in my studio, and I put the video on my television, and I sit on my couch, and I have a controller in my hands that is not even plugged in, right? It's just there, and I sit back on my couch and I start imagining myself as a player playing the game for the first time. The reason I'm doing this is I'm trying to find the most perfect tempo for what the music should be to match what I'm seeing. Then I have a little metronome app on my phone which is sitting on my thigh, and I will literally tap metronome tempos and write them in a notebook and say, "This level needs to be 99 beats per minute. This level needs to be 138. This one needs to be 216 beats per minute." And the whole reason I'm doing that is to try and find a tempo that fits with the natural pace of the gameplay itself.

I have to do that because if the music I make is too fast, it becomes overwhelming and annoying to the player. At that point, players go into the options menu and they turn the music down or off. And if they're doing that, I have completely failed. Not just at my job, but at life in general. If my music is too slow, that can result in reviewers saying, "This game feels sluggish. This game feels slow. The game itself didn't quite feel exciting." You know what I mean? That even if the game is tight, even if the game feels really good, the mechanics are there, everything is really nice and polished, if the music is too slow, the whole experience can feel really sluggish, you know?

So, my job is to just find the right tempo. Once I've got the tempo, then everything can get built from that point there. I set everything in my studio up to that tempo, and then I start building ideas out to match the game itself.

IGN: Once the developers of Boltgun 2 have given you artwork and gameplay videos, do you just lock yourself in your studio and produce the track on your own? Was there much back and forth with the development team?

Gordon: It's definitely a back and forth thing. I mean, you've got to understand when I start working on a project, there's nothing. Nothing exists. It's a complete blank canvas, you know? I don't even have a sharpened pencil at that point. It's nothing. And I get nothing for free. Like nothing. Nobody comes along and says, "Make this in D minor at 90 beats per minute" or whatever. Nothing. Nothing at all.

I have to experiment. I have to try. And I'm very big on finding teams and people that I love working with that I can feel comfortable in failure with. So, when I am submitting an idea, I have more confidence in myself submitting an idea that might be a stupid idea or might be an extreme idea. It might be a crazy idea because I need the team to be able to start saying yes or no to certain things. It's definitely a collaboration that I have with them. Like anybody does with a computer-based setup, [I have] millions of possibilities. I can do anything. I can do an entire video game score on [a] laptop if I need to. Anything is possible these days.

What happens with that freedom is choice paralysis. There's a million different decisions that need to get made all the damn time. And when I'm faced with a branching path between decision A or decision B, I need a deciding factor of which way to go. Now, I can do a lot of that on my own end, for sure, with my own taste, my own input, but at some point I'm going to need to say to somebody who's a lot closer to the project, who's been on it for a number of years, "Hey, do you prefer A or B or C or D or A," whatever it is.

So, there's definitely that back and forth process, and I love that, too. I love that because it starts involving them, and they start feeling like they're part of the music, and their input starts developing and shaping the song as a whole as well.

IGN: Is it a unique challenge to be tasked with specifically soundtracking what is effectively the climax of the game? Where your job is to basically push the peak of the player’s experience to its absolute limits?

Gordon: It is, but it also taps into this rather unsavory part of my personality, which is the desire to walk into a room and be the absolute most arrogant bastard in the place. And when we're in the final boss battle, I can walk in and be the loudest, most obnoxious bastard in the room.

IGN: That sounds like fun [laughs]. Is it also somewhat bittersweet in another sense, given that your music isn’t featured until the end of Boltgun 2, and statistically that’s likely to be a point that only a fraction of the audience will actually reach?

Gordon: Yeah, that's a really good point. When I make this massive game score, I know that there's a large percentage of players that are never going to hear this little bit of music. There's music I have in games that I know from even Doom and stuff that people have never, [or] very rarely even heard. The whole Rip & Tear track, for example, is about 28 minutes long. The version that sits on the album is what, three minutes or something like that? I had to cut out so much stuff just to fit it on Spotify. There's so much to it that people will only hear if they do something really specific and really unique.

But I love that, too, because I love that feeling that I had when I was playing games as a kid of finding a hidden area or finding something secret. It made it feel like I had a closer relationship to the game, you know? It felt like it had a little secret thing, and I knew that little secret now. [It meant that] the game and I now had a bit more of a deeper relationship, you know?

And so I love the fact that there's only going to be a small percentage, and it is—when you look at the actual numbers on Steam or whatever, it can be like 6% of people get to the boss battle. It's crazy, [but] I don't care. I love that. I think that's actually really cool because for those 6% of people that will get it, they'll get something that's specific and unique. You know what I mean? And I get to build a relationship with that player that the rest of the population doesn't have. I think that's really quite special.

IGN: Speaking of Doom, your work on that series was so remarkable because it became something beyond merely background music, it actually had an active influence on the player. Like the rhythm of the music basically dictated the rhythm of the action and vice versa. It was like a perpetual motion machine. Is that the absolute ideal for you? That your compositions will literally ride shotgun with the player?

Gordon: Yeah. The term I like is "forward momentum." I love that games, I feel, are the only art form where there is a direct link between the audience and the art form itself. If I'm in an art gallery, there is a gap between the canvas and me, the viewer. If I'm watching a film, there is a gap between the film itself and me sitting on the couch. But a game only works if you, the player, are interacting with it. Without that, the game is useless. It doesn't do anything. It needs your input.

So, there is this cyclical thing between you and the game. This cycle that you work back and forward. The player is a collaborator. It's very important. If you take out the player, the game doesn't exist. It's absolutely useless. You need that. So, I'm always trying to think about how that works.

Now, it doesn't just work philosophically. It works on a technical level. My music for a game is essentially a three or a four or a five-hour song. It's one song. It exists in one session. That song gets broken up into multiple little segments that then get rearranged based on what the player is doing. If the player is low on health, if they're into the next level, if they're fighting a boss, if they're doing really well, if they're not doing really well, if they're in a tutorial… Whatever it is, if they're playing with their friends, the music will change based on what they're doing. They are literally in control. They're the conductor. So, there is always going to be that relationship between what I'm doing and the player. That's absolutely super important. And that's always in the back of my mind. I can't escape it. That is literally the nature of video games.

Warhammer 40K: Boltgun 2 is out now on PlayStation 5, PC, and Xbox Series X|S, with a Nintendo Switch 2 version to be released at a later date. You can check out IGN’s review of the retro-styled first-person shooter sequel here , where we gave it 8 out of 10 and declared it was “an explosive sequel that packs a bloody punch.”

He has 25 years of experience covering video games, having served as Deputy Editor on Official PlayStation 2 Magazine Australia and as Editor of Official Xbox 360 Magazine Australia, before joining IGN in 2009. articles.title: The Street Fighter Cast Would Love to Make a Mortal Kombat Crossover Movie
articles.summary: I got the chance to chat with the cast of the Street Fighter movie ahead of its theatrical release, and almost all of them are game for a crossover film with Mortal Kombat.
articles.body:
I got the chance to chat with the cast of the Street Fighter movie ahead of its theatrical release, and almost all of them are game for a crossover film with Mortal Kombat.

In May 2026, Mortal Kombat co-creator Ed Boon posted about wanting a Street Fighter guest character in a Mortal Kombat game, saying he was a “huge fan” of Capcom’s flagship fighting game franchise.

Given that Mortal Kombat II released in theaters earlier this year, I had to ask the actors starring in the Street Fighter movie if they’d be willing to throw down with the likes of Shao Kahn to protect Earthrealm alongside Liu Kang and co. — and the consensus was a resounding “yes.”

In fact, Andrew Schulz joked that he was trying to make this collaboration happen with his viral joke at the 2025 Game Awards, where he famously took shots at the cast of Mortal Kombat II.

“This is what we were trying to do at [The Game Awards]!” Schulz told me. “We’re trying to set this thing up!”

“That’s what we were trying to do,” Cody Rhodes added.

“Tell them I know Noob Saibot which is [Ed Boon's and John Tobias’] names backwards,” Eric Andre interjected. “...but a crossover? A Flinstones/Jetsons crossover? We’re in. Let’s go.”

Andrew Koji, Noah Centineo, and Callina Liang were also enthusiastic about the idea. Koji specifically mentioned Marvel vs Capcom as another possible crossover opportunity… though the likelihood of this particular partnership happening is looking astronomically low .

“Hell yeah,” Koji said to the Mortal Kombat idea. “I said yes, because I’ve got friends in Mortal Kombat.”

“See, he’s got friends that worked on Mortal Kombat, so he’s trying to play nice over there,” Centineo joked.

“I love the girl who plays Kitana,” Liang said. “I’ve met Adeline a few times. She’s awesome.”

“That’d be sick,” Koji continued. “But then there’s Marvel vs Capcom. We’ve gotta tap into that.”

“Here’s what I want — I want more Street Fighter,” Centineo said. “If you bring an opportunity to us to be able to come back and reup these incredible characters, I’m down, and I know we’re all down. So if that’s Mortal Kombat, if that’s me kicking Thor in his face, you know?”

Marvel vs Capcom Screenshots - Nintendo Direct June 2024

Of course, a Mortal Kombat x Street Fighter film might be a bit tricky, given that Mel Jarnson plays a character in both movies. I asked her about the possibility of such a project on the red carpet at the Street Fighter movie premier, and even though it’d be a bit of a challenge, she was more than willing to take on.

“It would be epic!” she said. “And you would bring Nitara back to life. Sew her back up. She’d be like half-blonde, with a wing. Half-Cammy, half-Nitara.”

For now, it remains to be seen if there’s real potential for a wacky crossover movie with these two fighting game series — but if the stars align, everyone seems pretty enthusiastic about it. And given both franchises’ wealth of guest characters and crossover games over the years, it wouldn’t exactly be uncharted territory.

Street Fighter releases in theaters on Friday, October 16, 2026.

articles.title: Callina Liang Says She Felt 'A Lot of Pressure' After Seeing How Reddit Reacted to Her Being Cast as Chun-Li
articles.summary: Callina Liang admitted that she felt a ton of pressure after she saw fans’ reactions to her getting cast as Chun-Li in the Street Fighter movie, specifically mentioning a thread she saw on Reddit.
articles.body:
Callina Liang admitted that she felt a ton of pressure after she saw fans’ reactions to the news of her getting cast as Chun-Li in the Street Fighter movie, specifically mentioning a thread she saw on Reddit.

Yes, celebrities actually read what you say about them on the internet. Speaking with Project Big Screen , Liang revealed what went through her mind after she saw what fans were saying about her on Reddit when Deadline broke the news that she got cast as Chun-Li. And surprisingly, she has a lot more in common with the fighting game community than you might think.

“There was this Reddit thread: ‘Callina Liang’s thighs are nowhere as big as Chun-Li’s,’” she laughed. “But like, absolutely. When I look at it, as a huge fan myself, I would want whoever plays Chun-Li to be what I envision her to be in my head, and what you see of her in the video games and in the anime. She looks insane. Her body is insane.”

But Liang knew her limits. With just two months to prepare for the role, she didn’t have much time to grow her thighs as big as the First Lady of Fighting Games — but she was determined to do her best with the time she had, while making sure to be realistic about her goals.

“I did feel a lot of pressure. I was like, ‘Right, I gotta get my s**t together.’ My motto the whole time was just, ‘No regrets. Give it your all. It doesn’t matter how big you can physically get.’ You know, I only had two months. I had to be realistic with myself. I had to be a functioning human being who could act on screen at the end of the day. If I went full-throttle with building my body a certain way, I probably wouldn’t be able to function normally.

“I was just like, 'Have zero regrets, try your best and some, and whatever result you end up with, you can say, at least I gave it my all.' That’s what I did, and I think I'm happy.”

Photos taken from set prove that Liang’s efforts paid off. In fact, the actress revealed that she ate a dozen eggs every single day, as well as a meal every two hours, in order to meet her calorie goals and grow her muscles — to the point where she almost threw up. It worked, though, as she was able to grow her thighs 6.5 centimeters each. Even her stunt double couldn't keep up, who had to wear butt pads in order to realistically sell the idea that she and Liang were the same person in the film.

"Chun-Li is all kicks. So we did a bunch of Taekwondo training, Muay Thai, and Wushu (Kung Fu). I did two hours of that a day and strengthened my legs a lot and changed my diet drastically. When I was bulking, I ate 12 eggs a day. Every two hours I had to have a meal, and I was on the verge of throwing up. But it worked. By the end of the shoot, my thighs had grown six-and-a-half centimeters each,” she said in an August interview with Empire Magazine.

You can catch Liang’s martial arts skills firsthand in the Street Fighter movie , which releases in theaters this Friday, October 16.

articles.title: League Championship Series Day Four Game Thread
articles.summary: Time for NLCS Game 3
articles.body:
Last night, the American League (AL) Championship Series took center stage, while the National League (NL) Championship Series was off for a scheduled travel day.

After losing Game 1 at home to the Cleveland Guardians, the Tampa Bay Rays bounced back with a 3-1 victory to even the series at one apiece heading into the next three games in Cleveland. The outcome may have been different if Guardians third baseman José Ramírez had fielded a ground ball cleanly instead of letting it slip through his legs, allowing the Rays to score the first run of a three-run fourth inning.

Today, the schedule shifts, with Game 3 between the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Milwaukee Brewers the only game on the slate.

After winning the first two games of this best-of-seven affair, the Brewers enter this evening's matchup in Los Angeles two wins away from dethroning the Dodgers and claiming just their second NL pennant in franchise history.

The Dodgers, who are chasing a historic three-peat, will not go quietly. Given that the teams were the two best in the NL this season, it would not be surprising if the NLCS returns to Milwaukee for Game 6, and if necessary, a win-or-go-home Game 7.

Brewers left-hander Robert Gasser will make his second career postseason start tonight. The 27-year-old started Game 4 of the Division Series against the San Diego Padres, receiving a no-decision after allowing one run on three hits over four innings. Will Gasser deliver a second consecutive strong postseason outing, or will the Dodgers' offense rattle the southpaw and force Milwaukee to turn to its bullpen earlier than expected?

Gasser's counterpart, Dodgers left-hander Blake Snell, has considerably more postseason experience. The veteran southpaw will make his second start of this postseason and 17th of his career. Snell started Game 2 of the Division Series against the Atlanta Braves, receiving a no-decision after allowing one run on three hits and five walks in 3 2/3 innings.

Following right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto's shortest career postseason start in Game 2, the Dodgers need a quality start from Snell to begin their comeback. However, another subpar outing could put Los Angeles on the brink of elimination.

What are your predictions for this game? Will Shohei Ohtani finally break out of his slump, or will the Brewers contain the Dodgers' offense once again?
